Hands on the Wheel, Phone in the Glovebox

Almost everyone I know carries a phone, and almost everyone I know has looked at it while driving. That includes me. A phone feels harmless in the car because nothing bad happens most of the time. You glance down, you glance up, the road is still there. I think that experience is exactly what makes phones so dangerous behind the wheel, and it is why I believe drivers should not be allowed to use them while the vehicle is moving, with a narrow exception for emergencies and for navigation that is set up before the trip begins.

The basic problem is that driving asks for three things at once: eyes on the road, hands on the wheel, and a mind that is paying attention. Texting takes away all three. A car traveling at highway speed covers roughly the length of a football field in the five seconds it takes to read a message. For that whole distance the driver is effectively blindfolded. A child stepping off a curb, a car braking ahead, a light turning red: none of these wait for someone to finish typing "on my way." Federal safety officials have attributed thousands of deaths every year in the United States to distracted driving, and phones are one of the biggest sources of that distraction.

Some people argue that the answer is hands-free technology. If the phone is mounted on the dashboard and the driver speaks instead of types, the hands and eyes stay where they belong. This is better than texting, but it does not solve the third problem. Researchers who study attention have found that a driver deep in a phone conversation can look straight at something and fail to register it. The conversation occupies the part of the brain that would otherwise be scanning for hazards. A passenger in the car is different, because a passenger can see the traffic and will usually stop talking when things get tense. The person on the other end of a call has no idea that the driver is merging onto a crowded freeway.

There is also a fairness argument. When a driver chooses to use a phone, the driver is not the only one taking the risk. Pedestrians, cyclists, passengers, and people in other cars never agreed to it. We already accept this reasoning for drunk driving. Nobody says a person has the right to drive after six beers as long as they feel fine, because the cost of being wrong falls on strangers. A driver reading a text can be just as impaired, for those few seconds, as one who has been drinking.

I do not think the rule has to be absolute in every situation. A driver who witnesses a crash or is being followed should be able to call for help. Navigation apps are useful too, and a voice that says "turn left in half a mile" is probably safer than a driver squinting at street signs or unfolding a paper map. The key is that the destination gets entered while the car is parked. If the route needs to change, the driver can pull over. The same goes for music: pick the playlist before shifting into drive.

Critics will say such laws are hard to enforce, and they are right that police cannot see into every car. But laws do more than punish. Seat belt laws were also hard to enforce at first, and over time they changed what people considered normal. A clear ban tells new drivers, especially teenagers who have grown up with a phone in their hand, that the message can wait.

Every call and text will still be there when the car is parked. A life taken in a crash will not come back. Given that trade, asking drivers to put the phone away is a small request.
